https://www.newvision.co.ug/category/wor.text: Warsaw and Kyiv exhume Volyn victims at centre of diplomatic quarrel Disagreements over what happened and who is responsible for the Volyn massacres have long cast a shadow over ties between the otherwise now close neighbours. ________________ UKRAINE - Beneath two now-deserted villages in western Ukraine –- the site of WWII-era massacres, archaeologists are uncovering the bones at the heart of a dispute that has strained relations between Warsaw and Kyiv for years. Disagreements over what happened and who is responsible for the Volyn massacres have long cast a shadow over ties between the otherwise now close neighbours. Between 1943 and 1945, some 70,000-100,000 civilians were killed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) in territory occupied by Nazi Germany, according to Polish estimates of the toll. Warsaw calls it a "genocide" against the Polish minority, while Ukraine hails the UPA as freedom fighters, sees the events as a wartime "tragedy" and says that Ukrainians were killed in retaliation. Amid sunflower fields and forests, joint Polish-Ukrainian teams of archaeologists have been carefully excavating the remains of victims. "We want to restore their first and last names ... to fulfil the duty that rests on us as heirs of those who were murdered here," said Karol Polejowski, deputy president of the head of Poland's Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). The remains of over 50 people have been recovered in a series of exhumations taking place in the area, but they have yet to be identified. A handmade wooden cross, planted near the graves, is one of the few signs that the villages ever existed. Political leaders in both countries believe the exhumations can be a first step in repairing relations, which have been strained this year by a row triggered when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the UPA. 'Civilian population' In a white tent around 10 kilometres (six miles) from the Polish border, experts meticulously lay out the skeletons of recovered victims, measuring bones and carefully trying to match broken skull fragments. A small number of other artefacts -- rosaries, religious medallions and shoes -- have also been unearthed under the field of yellow-and-black sunflowers, one of the national symbols of Ukraine. "The remains were arranged in a highly disordered manner. Most of the bodies had been brought to the burial pit and simply dumped into it," Olga Mineiko, an anthropologist at the Ukrainian Memorial and Search Center, told AFP on the site. The victims were likely "driven to the field of death barefoot and without personal belongings," said Polejowski. The genetic material is collected, with the IPN appealing to Poles who believe they may have lost relatives in the massacre to provide their own to help find matches. Forensic specialists and anthropologists will also examine the bones to determine the approximate age, sex and cause of death of each of them. It is believed that between 30 to 40 percent of the 50 remains so far discovered at the site were children, according to Polejowski. Diplomatic spat The massacres have been a recurring point of contention between Warsaw and Kyiv. The UPA was a paramilitary organisation tied to the Ukrainian independence movement that fought the Soviet Union's Red Army. But it collaborated with the Nazis when they first invaded the Soviet Union, clashed with the Polish resistance and killed Poles, Jews and other civilians. Since Russia invaded in 2022, the UPA has been honoured in Ukraine as a force that fought for independence from Moscow under the Soviet Union. Kyiv insisted Zelensky's choice of name for the military unit was not directed against Warsaw. But Polish President Karol Nawrocki withdrew Poland's highest national honour from him in response. In Poland, the issue has become even more politicised as nationalist parties seek to embolden their base ahead of parliamentary elections next year, part of a broader campaign to whip up anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Poland is home to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian refugees, with a backlash against their presence having surged during a divisive presidential election campaign last year, won by the right-wing Nawrocki. The country is still the main hub for military and humanitarian aid deliveries to Ukraine, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-European government has repeatedly called for a de-escalation. Warsaw has welcomed efforts by Zelensky to cool the tension, including the promise of opening of classified intelligence documents. As Tusk and Zelensky try to bury the hatchet, in the Ukrainian fields near the Polish border, plans are underway for a proper farewell to those uncovered. "We want them to be buried here, where they lived, where each of them had their dreams and plans, and wanted their life to unfold," said Polejowski. "In this soil they should rest." Help us improve! https://www.popularmechanics.com/science.text: Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:As Europe experiences extreme heatwaves, electricity generation is coming under strain.One area of concern is nuclear power, which partially relies on river water to cool its reactors—something that’s in short supply at the moment. Despite some reactors shutting down either partially or entirely, nuclear power remains relatively resilient compared to other forms of electricity generation.The extensive and punishing drought impacting Europe this summer is an ominous specter of things to come. Sweltering temperatures have spiked electricity demand, and thousands have died from heat-related causes. And just as millions of Europeans are rushing to crank the A/C (if they have access to it at all), the systems that supply the power for those life-saving machines are faltering under intense heat and prolonged water shortages.One of the industries that has been most acutely impacted by the oppressive heat is nuclear energy, since several important reactors rely on river water to keep cool. The problem with that methodology is two-fold: Depending on the case, water levels are too low to use rivers as a cooling mechanism and/or the water itself is too warm. For example, the two-gigawatt Paks nuclear plant in Hungary, responsible for nearly half of the country’s electricity output, shut down half of its turbines due to record-low water levels. Meanwhile, the Beznau nuclear plant in northern Switzerland went offline in response to high river temperatures.While these shutdowns are worrisome for the future viability of nuclear power in certain parts of Europe, the problem isn’t a full-scale disaster yet. According to Carbon Brief, only 14 percent of the 440 nuclear reactors around the world are cooled using rivers, and Michael Tadrous, a researcher at McMaster University in Canada, said that even these shutdowns have little impact in terms of output.“Warmer intake water makes a reactor slightly less efficient. [But] even an extreme 15C rise in cooling-water temperature would cost a large reactor only about 6% of its output,” Tadrous told Carbon Brief. “The real pressure point during a heatwave is usually legal rather than technical. Plants return their cooling water to the river a few degrees warmer than they drew it and the law limits how warm that water may be in order to protect aquatic life.”Warm river temperatures can usually recover quickly once heatwaves pass, but low water levels require more rain to return to ideal operating levels. And the latter situation is one of Europe’s biggest problems right now—there’s no rain in sight.Of course, this isn’t an unknown risk for nuclear power in Europe. France—which gets about 70 percent of its energy from nuclear fission—shut down plants just last year (and many prior years), and in July 2026, turned off three of its 57 power plants, resulting in an approximately 9 percent reduction in energy production. However, these reductions usually represent no more than one percent of total annual electrical output.Tadrous, the lead author of a new study in the journal Energy Policy, analyzed the efficiency of nuclear power in a steadily warming world and found, along with his co-authors, that the addition of cooling towers, dry-air systems, and smart outages have curtailed nuclear energy losses by a staggering 91 percent since 2003. Analyzing heatwaves in 2022 in Europe, the authors also noted that nuclear power continued to run at 90 percent capacity, which was about 10 times steadier that other renewable sources, such as wind and solar.“Our expanded analysis demonstrates that while these challenges are real, they do not warrant the broad conclusion that riverine nuclear power is inherently unsustainable,” the authors wrote. “Historical evidence reveals that nuclear fleets have consistently exhibited high levels of reliability, even under extreme weather conditions, with only modest reductions in output during the most severe events.”Tackling the climate crisis requires every tool in humanity’s arsenal, and for the increasingly Sun-scorched summers in Europe, nuclear energy will likely continue to play a major role well into the future.
